paragraphs: The creator, as the ground of all reality, infinitely transcends all of creation: no finite mind can comprehend the infinite, and no created thing can equal the creator. Yet transcendence is not absence—all of creation points beyond itself toward its source.

Transcendence, however, does not mean hiddenness. Creation bears the emanations of the creator—such as intelligence, beauty, goodness, order, and harmony—imprinted on all that exists. Just as a craftsman’s nature is visible in the work of their hands, the creator’s character is disclosed through the structures, laws, and forms woven into creation. The creator is thus knowable through what has been made: creation is the expression, the trace, and the outward face of its source.

Across traditions, this conviction runs deep. Paul writes that the creator’s invisible nature “has been understood and seen through the things he has made” [19]. Plotinus traces the One’s overflow into Intellect, then Soul, then Matter, bearing the creator’s mark at each stage [11]; Bonaventure finds in every creature a vestigium—a footprint of the divine [22]. The Kabbalistic Sefirot names ten divine emanations through which the infinite Ein Sof discloses itself in creation [50]. From the East, Laozi teaches that the Tao, though nameless, is known through its De—its virtue flowing outward through all things [30]. Together, these voices confirm one truth: the creator cannot be fully grasped, yet is everywhere disclosed through creation’s fabric— known not by direct sight, but by the light it casts on all that exists.
